questions.prompt: Assess this claim: A model that fits for inference necessarily fits for training.
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: False

Weights are only part of training memory: gradients, optimizer states, master weights, activations and temporary buffers also consume VRAM. A 70B model needs about 140 GB for two-byte weights alone, before runtime overhead. FP32, FP16, BF16 and FP8 trade range and precision; hardware and kernels determine usable support.
keyPoints: Weights are only part of training memory: gradients, optimizer states, master weights, activations and temporary buffers also consume VRAM.
A 70B model needs about 140 GB for two-byte weights alone, before runtime overhead.
FP32, FP16, BF16 and FP8 trade range and precision; hardware and kernels determine usable support.

questions.prompt: Assess this claim: DDP replicates model state and all-reduces gradients.
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: True

DDP replicates model state and all-reduces gradients. FSDP and ZeRO shard different combinations of parameters, gradients and optimizer state. Tensor parallelism splits operations, pipeline parallelism splits layers, and expert parallelism distributes MoE experts. NCCL provides GPU communication collectives; interconnect bandwidth can dominate multi-node runs.
keyPoints: DDP replicates model state and all-reduces gradients.
FSDP and ZeRO shard different combinations of parameters, gradients and optimizer state.
Tensor parallelism splits operations, pipeline parallelism splits layers, and expert parallelism distributes MoE experts.
NCCL provides GPU communication collectives; interconnect bandwidth can dominate multi-node runs.

questions.prompt: Assess this claim: Saving only model weights is enough for an exact training restart.
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: False

Gradient accumulation increases effective batch size without retaining every microbatch activation. Gradient checkpointing recomputes activations to save memory. DeepSpeed and Accelerate help orchestrate training, but do not eliminate configuration and profiling work. Durable checkpoints need optimizer, scheduler, data position and random-number state as well as weights.
keyPoints: Gradient accumulation increases effective batch size without retaining every microbatch activation.
Gradient checkpointing recomputes activations to save memory.
DeepSpeed and Accelerate help orchestrate training, but do not eliminate configuration and profiling work.
Durable checkpoints need optimizer, scheduler, data position and random-number state as well as weights.

questions.prompt: Adding GPUs barely improves training throughput. What would you inspect first, and why?
questions.referenceAnswer: Profile communication time and data loading. Inspect synchronization and interconnect bandwidth. Compare scaling at a fixed global batch size and report utilization.
keyPoints: Profile communication time and data loading.
Inspect synchronization and interconnect bandwidth.
Compare scaling at a fixed global batch size and report utilization.

questions.prompt: How would you test that the change fixed this incident rather than hiding it?
questions.referenceAnswer: Keep a reproducible failing case for this incident. Compare scaling at a fixed global batch size and report utilization. Compare the same workload before and after the change; record both the target metric and regressions.
keyPoints: Compare scaling at a fixed global batch size and report utilization.
Compare the same workload before and after the change.
Check regressions as well as the target metric.

questions.prompt: The fix works in a small test but fails at production scale. What next?
questions.referenceAnswer: Profile communication time and data loading. Measure representative workloads and separate resource, data and configuration differences. Stage a rollout with a rollback condition and rerun the original failure case.
keyPoints: Profile communication time and data loading.
Measure a representative workload.
Stage rollout and define rollback criteria.

questions.prompt:
A small operation repeatedly reading large arrays can be bandwidth-bound even on a powerful GPU.

What principle should guide the decision in this situation, and why?
questions.referenceAnswer:
A GPU workload can be limited by arithmetic, memory movement, or communication. Arithmetic intensity relates operations to data moved. Larger theoretical compute does not help a workload stalled on memory or input preparation. Profiling identifies which resource actually limits the step.

Optimize the measured resource bottleneck rather than peak compute alone.
keyPoints: Optimize the measured resource bottleneck rather than peak compute alone.
A GPU workload can be limited by arithmetic, memory movement, or communication.

questions.prompt:
Two-byte weights for 7B parameters need about 14 decimal GB before gradients or optimizer states.

What principle should guide the decision in this situation, and why?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Training memory includes parameters, gradients, optimizer states, activations, and temporary buffers. Precision and optimizer implementation change bytes per parameter. Estimate these components separately and include allocator headroom; a weights-only estimate describes neither full training nor reliable deployment capacity.

State assumptions for each memory component and reserve runtime headroom.
keyPoints: State assumptions for each memory component and reserve runtime headroom.
Training memory includes parameters, gradients, optimizer states, activations, and temporary buffers.

questions.prompt:
Eight ranks with four examples and two accumulation steps produce 64 examples per update.

What principle should guide the decision in this situation, and why?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Effective batch size depends on local examples, data-parallel ranks, and accumulation steps. This arithmetic assumes the intended data partitioning and loss weighting. Changing world size without adjusting other settings changes optimization and may invalidate a speed comparison.

Hold optimization conditions explicit when comparing distributed configurations.
keyPoints: Hold optimization conditions explicit when comparing distributed configurations.
Effective batch size depends on local examples, data-parallel ranks, and accumulation steps.

questions.prompt:
A short final microbatch should not receive the same total weight as a much larger one when optimizing mean per-example loss.

What principle should guide the decision in this situation, and why?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Accumulation sums gradients across microbatches before an optimizer step. Normalize losses according to the intended global mean, especially with unequal microbatch or token counts. Gradient synchronization frequency also affects performance and must match the accumulation design.

Weight accumulated contributions by the intended example or token denominator.
keyPoints: Weight accumulated contributions by the intended example or token denominator.
Accumulation sums gradients across microbatches before an optimizer step.

questions.prompt:
One rank skipping backward while peers enter a gradient collective can stall the job.

What principle should guide the decision in this situation, and why?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Data parallel ranks process different data with replicated model state and combine gradients. All ranks must execute compatible collectives; divergent control flow can hang synchronization. Data sampling and loss weighting determine whether the combined update matches the intended objective.

Collective participation and ordering must agree across ranks.
keyPoints: Collective participation and ordering must agree across ranks.
Data parallel ranks process different data with replicated model state and combine gradients.

questions.prompt:
A bucket that becomes ready only at the end of backward offers little overlap.

What principle should guide the decision in this situation, and why?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Gradient communication can overlap backward computation when gradients become ready in groups. Bucket sizing trades launch overhead against the opportunity to start communication early. Model structure and network bandwidth influence the useful configuration; tuning needs a timeline profile.

Tune overlap from readiness and communication timelines.
keyPoints: Tune overlap from readiness and communication timelines.
Gradient communication can overlap backward computation when gradients become ready in groups.

questions.prompt:
Splitting a matrix operation may require reducing partial outputs before the next layer.

What principle should guide the decision in this situation, and why?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Tensor parallelism divides parts of a layer's computation across devices. The partition determines where partial results must be combined or exchanged. Frequent communication makes interconnect topology important; spreading tightly coupled shards across slow links can erase compute gains.

Choose partitions with their communication requirements and topology in mind.
keyPoints: Choose partitions with their communication requirements and topology in mind.
Tensor parallelism divides parts of a layer's computation across devices.

questions.prompt:
A much slower middle stage makes neighboring devices wait even when layer counts are equal.

What principle should guide the decision in this situation, and why?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Pipeline parallelism places layer groups on different devices and schedules microbatches through them. Fill and drain periods create bubbles. Balancing stage cost and increasing useful in-flight work can help, but memory and scheduling complexity limit the design.

Balance measured stage cost rather than only layer count.
keyPoints: Balance measured stage cost rather than only layer count.
Pipeline parallelism places layer groups on different devices and schedules microbatches through them.

questions.prompt:
Two processes assigned the same global rank can prevent correct group formation.

What principle should guide the decision in this situation, and why?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Distributed startup needs consistent membership, rank identities, and communication endpoints. Configuration errors can resemble model failures. Validate connectivity and a minimal collective before running a full training job, and record the environment needed to reproduce the launch.

Validate group membership and connectivity with a minimal distributed test.
keyPoints: Validate group membership and connectivity with a minimal distributed test.
Distributed startup needs consistent membership, rank identities, and communication endpoints.

questions.prompt:
Extending a timeout may merely make a mismatched collective hang for longer.

What principle should guide the decision in this situation, and why?
questions.referenceAnswer:
GPU collectives can hang because of mismatched calls, device failures, or network problems. Collect logs and rank-local timelines, then reduce the workload to a minimal reproduction. Treat timeout changes as diagnostic controls rather than proof that the underlying issue is solved.

Compare rank participation and logs before only increasing timeouts.
keyPoints: Compare rank participation and logs before only increasing timeouts.
GPU collectives can hang because of mismatched calls, device failures, or network problems.

questions.prompt:
Doubling devices while also doubling batch size measures a different regime from holding the same job fixed.

What principle should guide the decision in this situation, and why?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Report useful examples or tokens per second with the workload definition. Scaling efficiency compares observed speedup with added resources under a chosen scaling regime. Strong scaling keeps total work fixed; weak scaling grows work with resources. Do not mix them silently.

State whether work and optimization conditions were held fixed.
keyPoints: State whether work and optimization conditions were held fixed.
Report useful examples or tokens per second with the workload definition.

questions.prompt:
One rank repeatedly receiving longer sequences can slow every synchronized step.

What principle should guide the decision in this situation, and why?
questions.referenceAnswer:
A synchronous job often waits for its slowest rank. Uneven sequence lengths, data loading, storage, or hardware can create stragglers. Compare rank-level timing distributions and batch characteristics before changing collective libraries or adding devices.

Investigate rank-level imbalance rather than only average step time.
keyPoints: Investigate rank-level imbalance rather than only average step time.
A synchronous job often waits for its slowest rank.
